q-126611.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14133198/assets/b6deaf63a158a3629a59ef3c86535681e490a08846dc6fed493d64cd788b8166.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{1}{y}$ that lies between $y=1$ and $y=2,$ as shown above. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
q-126611.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{y})=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\sqrt{{y}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the arc of the curve x=1y that lies between y=1 and y=2, as shown above. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
 2π∫121yy2+1dy
b
 2π∫121y3y2+1ydy
c
 2π∫121y3y4+1dy
d
 2π∫121y2y4+1ydy
e
 2π∫121y2y4+1dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2x1+(dxdy)2dy.

We are told that the limits of integration are from y=1 to y=2.

Computing the derivative, we get

dxdy=ddy(1y)=−1y2

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({e}^{y})={e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14133198/assets/e8a154593153ff224bae3f334bd20e74c2513dab8a60e1482c98a99677b1f882.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}$ that lies in the first quadrant between $x=0$ and its $x$-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
q-109323.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ 9-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{\frac{9}{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{3x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since we're given a curve in the form y=f(x), we have

ds=1+(dydx)2dx.

Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫x1x2x1+(dydx)2dx.

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the x-axis by solving the following equation:

Computing the derivative, we get

dydx=ddx(9−x2)=−x9−x2.

Finally, we obtain

q-126712.name: Question 4
q-126712.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=4.$ What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
q-126712.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}x\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}x\sqrt{\frac{4x+1}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{x(4x+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the arc of the curve y=x that lies between the lines x=0 and x=4. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
2π∫04x2+xdx
b
π∫044x+1dx
c
π∫04x4x+1dx
d
π∫044x2+xdx
e
2π∫04x4x2+xdx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since we're given a curve in the form y=f(x), we have

ds=1+(dydx)2dx.

Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫x1x2x1+(dydx)2dx.

Computing the derivative, we get

dydx=ddx(x)=12x.

Finally, we obtain

S=2π∫x1x2x1+(dydx)2dx=2π∫04x1+(12x)2dx=2π∫04x1+14xdx=2π∫04x4x+14xdx=π∫04x(4x+1)dx=π∫044x2+xdx.

q-109409.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y={x}^{2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
q-109409.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+4{x}^{2}.$ Then, $x\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}(\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{[\frac{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}{3}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{9}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
